subjects.displayTitle: Education of children: discovering the treasures within
subjects.introduction: Education begins here with a striking claim: the human being contains treasures whose discovery requires care. The opening passages invite us to see a child’s possibilities, to respond patiently to immaturity, and to make kindness a habit extending even to animals. Learning then unfolds across the whole of life: the sciences and arts, useful work, the love of beauty, spiritual understanding and the ability to live well with others. The educator’s manner belongs to this work as fully as the lesson itself; encouragement, example, play and attention to aptitude sit beside the demand for effort and a developing sense of responsibility. This vision reaches beyond the household. The education of girls, support for orphans and children without means, and the preparation and sustenance of teachers make the school a concern of the community. Neighboring subjects on capacity, curricula, family life, the advancement of women and universal education reveal how closely these responsibilities are connected. The collection also contains difficult historical descriptions and contrasting advice about particular schools. Its revealed provisions belong to their respective settings, and its letters and recorded conversations call for attention to audience, circumstance and source authority. Jesus’ welcome to children and Mencius’s image of growth damaged by repeated neglect offer further ways into the inquiry. What might change when we judge education by the persons it helps to develop, the dignity it protects and the peace those persons can learn to create?

questions: What do the images of gems, gardens and growing trees suggest about the relationship between a child’s capacities and the work of an educator? How do the passages about differing aptitudes complicate the expectations adults may bring to a child?

How might encouragement, joyful learning, example and firm moral expectations work together? What do the passages on patience, developmental readiness and the rejection of striking or vilifying children ask of the educator’s own character?

What becomes possible when sciences, arts, practical skills and spiritual formation enrich one another? How could an education deepen faith while cultivating inquiry, freedom from prejudice and service to people of every background?

How do the passages distribute responsibility among parents, relatives, teachers, institutions and the wider community? What would their concern for girls, orphans and children without means require in practice, and how do resources and local circumstances affect the response?

What new questions arise when you read Jesus’ welcome to children in Mark alongside Mencius’s account of damaged and renewed growth? Which similarities illuminate this compilation, and which differences in their accounts of human nature and spiritual life invite further study?

How might the everyday life of a family or school help cultivate peace and human unity? What other changes would need to accompany education, and which connected subject—such as the development of capacity, the role of women or universal education—would help you explore those relationships?

references.label: 1 · Mark 10:13–16 · Welcoming children and learning from them
references.note: Read the whole encounter in the King James Version. People bring children to Jesus, the disciples rebuke them, and Jesus welcomes and blesses the children while also speaking of receiving the Kingdom as a child. Compare this movement with the passages here that address children as members of the Kingdom and express hope for their education and service. What do adults owe to children, and what might adults need to learn from them? How do welcome, trust and spiritual growth relate in these texts? Attend to the Gospel’s particular account of the Kingdom while exploring the Bahá’í passages in their own setting.
references.verified: Read Mark 10:13–16 in full, King James Version, Bible Gateway, 2026-10-10. Verified the bringing of children, disciples’ rebuke, Jesus’ displeasure and welcome, receiving the Kingdom as a child, embrace and blessing.

references.label: 2 · Mencius 6A8 · Nourishment and the appearance of barrenness
references.note: In Gaozi I, section 8, read the passage on Niu Mountain in James Legge’s translation. Trees are cut down, new growth is browsed, and the resulting bare appearance is mistaken for the mountain’s original condition. Mencius uses this image to consider the human moral heart, its losses and its need for nourishment. Read it beside this compilation’s images of gardens and cultivation, its attention to acquired habits, and its insistence on patient education. How might a judgment about a child’s apparent capacity change when we attend to the conditions of growth? What would count as nourishment or repeated damage? Explore the shared imagery without assuming that Mencius and the Bahá’í texts give identical accounts of human nature.
